title: THE MAN WHO HAD SIXTY CHILDREN… AND SENT THIRTY DAUGHTERS AWAY TO MARRY OUTSIDE HIS FAMILY
paragraphs: THE MAN WHO HAD SIXTY CHILDREN… AND SENT THIRTY DAUGHTERS AWAY TO MARRY OUTSIDE HIS FAMILY

His name appears in only three verses of Scripture. He had thirty sons, thirty daughters, and sixty marriages connecting households. But behind this extraordinary family story is a question that reaches into our own homes: What are we building that will remain when our name is no longer spoken?
Imagine being remembered by the world for everything you owned, everything you accomplished, and everyone connected to your name…
But having almost nothing recorded about the condition of your soul.
Sixty children.
Thirty sons.
Thirty daughters.
An entire household large enough to fill a village gathering.
Weddings. Celebrations. Family alliances. Generations waiting to be born.
And yet, when God inspired the biblical account of this man's life, only three verses were written about him.
Three verses.
Not three chapters.
Not an entire book.
Just three verses to describe a man who once held authority over Israel.
His name was Ibzan.
What if your life is full of things people can count, but the things that matter most to God cannot be measured by numbers?
What if you have spent years building a family, a career, a reputation, or a ministry, only to discover that the greatest question was never how much you accumulated…
But whether your life was surrendered to the Lord?
That is where this forgotten judge of Israel becomes unexpectedly personal.
Because somewhere between his sixty children, his extraordinary marriage arrangements, and the silence surrounding his spiritual life, there is a lesson we desperately need to hear.
And it begins in Bethlehem.
Not necessarily the Bethlehem you are thinking of.
Judges 12:8–10 records:

“After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. And he had thirty sons, and thirty daughters, whom he sent abroad, and took in thirty daughters from abroad for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years. Then died Ibzan, and was buried at Bethlehem.”
— Judges 12:8–10, King James Version
Read that again.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters.
His daughters were married outside his immediate household, and he brought thirty women from outside into marriage with his sons.
Then he died.
That is the entire recorded account.
No dramatic battlefield.
No miraculous deliverance attributed specifically to him.
No lengthy speech.
No recorded prayer.
No explicit divine evaluation of his character.
Just a man, his family, his years of leadership, and his grave.
And sometimes, beloved, the silence of Scripture can make us examine questions we would rather avoid.
Because we are living in a generation obsessed with being noticed.
We want our accomplishments remembered.
We want our children successful.
We want our families respected.
We want our names associated with something impressive.
But Ibzan's story reminds us how quickly even an extraordinary earthly life can be summarized.
A man can have sixty children and still leave us wondering what he taught them about God.
A man can arrange sixty marriages and still leave us without a recorded testimony of what happened inside his own heart.
A man can judge Israel for seven years and still have no recorded words preserved from his mouth.
Now, we must be careful here.
The Bible does not say Ibzan was an ungodly father.
It does not accuse him of neglecting his children.
It does not tell us that his marriages were sinful.
It does not say he used his family for selfish political ambition.
We must never turn biblical silence into an accusation God did not make.
But we can allow that silence to ask us something.
If your life were summarized in three verses, what would those verses reveal?
Would they tell the world how much money you earned?
How many people admired you?
How many houses you built?
How many followers you gathered?
Or would someone be able to say that, despite your failures and struggles, you loved Jesus Christ and sought to make Him known?
There is something especially fascinating about the original Hebrew description of Ibzan's household.
Judges 12:9 says:
וַיְהִי־לוֹ שְׁלֹשִׁים בָּנִים וּשְׁלֹשִׁים בָּנוֹת
Vayhi-lo sheloshim banim usheloshim banot.
“And he had thirty sons and thirty daughters.”
Then the Hebrew describes the marriage arrangements with these words:
שִׁלַּח הַחוּצָה
Shillach hachutzah.
Literally, “he sent outside.”
And concerning the women brought in for his sons:
הֵבִיא לְבָנָיו מִן־הַחוּץ
Hevi levanav min-hachutz.
“He brought [them] for his sons from outside.”
The Hebrew emphasizes movement outward and inward.
Daughters sent out.
Daughters-in-law brought in.
A remarkable network of marriage connections.

These expressions are commonly understood as referring to marriages outside Ibzan's immediate family or household. The text does not establish that the spouses were foreigners, nor does it identify the specific families or communities involved.

Some interpreters have suggested that such marriages could have strengthened social relationships or alliances, which would be plausible in the world of ancient Israel. But Scripture does not explicitly tell us Ibzan's motives.
That distinction matters.
Because the purpose of studying the Bible is not to make the text say something dramatic.
It is to hear what God has actually given us.
And what He has given us is remarkable enough.
Sixty children.
Sixty marriages described or implied by the arrangements.
Seven years of judgeship.
One burial.
One brief record.
The Hebrew text then says:
וַיָּמָת אִבְצָן
Vayyamot Ivtsan.
“And Ibzan died.”
There it is.
The sentence no earthly power can prevent.
He died.
The man who once presided over an enormous household could not remain in that household forever.
The man who arranged marriages could not arrange his escape from mortality.
The man who judged Israel eventually came to the end of his own earthly life.
And suddenly, this ancient account does not feel so distant anymore.
Because we are all moving toward the same reality.
The father working overtime because he wants his children to have a better life.
The mother exhausted from caring for everyone while quietly wondering whether anyone notices her sacrifices.
The husband trying to provide but struggling to be emotionally present.
The wife praying for a marriage that looks peaceful in photographs but feels painfully lonely behind closed doors.
The young adult desperate to make the family proud.
The believer who appears spiritually strong in public but has been fighting secret battles with sin, shame, or discouragement.
We are all building something.
We are all spending our days on something.
And one day, the things we thought were permanent will pass into someone else's hands.
But there is a deeper danger than being forgotten by history.
It is living so distracted by temporary things that we neglect our relationship with the eternal God.
Jesus asked a question that cuts through every generation:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
— Mark 8:36, KJV
Think about that.
Not because having a large family is wrong.
Not because marriage is unimportant.
Not because earthly responsibility has no value.
Family is a gift from God. Marriage is honorable. Faithful parenting matters. Providing for one's household is a serious responsibility.
But even the greatest earthly blessings cannot replace the Savior.
You can provide your children with an education and still need to teach them the fear of the Lord.
You can give them beautiful wedding celebrations and still need to model repentance and forgiveness.
You can leave them property, savings, and opportunities while forgetting to speak to them about the grace that rescued your own soul.
And perhaps the most painful possibility is this:
Your children may remember everything you bought for them…
But struggle to remember a single moment when you humbly admitted you were wrong and asked for forgiveness.
That should reach every parent.
Not as condemnation.
As an invitation.
Because the Gospel is not merely about becoming a respectable person with a successful household.
It is about sinners being reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
And that changes the way we understand legacy.
Deuteronomy 6:6–7 commands God's people to keep His words in their hearts and diligently teach them to their children.
Notice the order.
The Word must first be in your own heart.
Before you can faithfully teach your children about walking with God, you must be willing to walk with Him yourself.
Before your family needs a perfect-looking Christian parent, they need an honest one who knows where forgiveness is found.
A father who says, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
A mother who says, “I am struggling too, but the Lord is helping me.”
A husband who stops using spiritual language to excuse his harshness.
A wife who brings her exhaustion to Christ rather than pretending she has unlimited strength.
A son or daughter who finally says, “I have been hiding something, and I need help.”
These moments may never be recorded in history books.
But they can become turning points in a family.
Sometimes the most powerful spiritual legacy begins with a broken voice saying:
“Jesus, I cannot keep pretending anymore.”
And that brings us to something beautiful about the place associated with Ibzan.
Bethlehem.
The Hebrew name is בֵּית לֶחֶם — Beit Lechem, commonly understood as “house of bread.”
Judges identifies Ibzan as being from Bethlehem and records that he was buried there.
Scholars debate whether his Bethlehem was the town in Judah or another Bethlehem associated with Zebulun. Scripture does not settle that identification beyond dispute.
So we should not confidently claim that Ibzan lived in the very town where Jesus would later be born.
But the name Bethlehem still brings a Christian reader's mind to one of the greatest moments in redemptive history.
Centuries after the period of the judges, the promised Messiah was born in Bethlehem of Judea.
And there is a striking contrast worth considering.
Ibzan's recorded life is marked by an extraordinary number of children and marriages.
Jesus entered the world in humility, born into a family without earthly grandeur.
Ibzan exercised authority over Israel for seven years.
Jesus is the eternal King whose kingdom will have no end.
Ibzan died and was buried.
Jesus died, was buried, and rose again on the third day.
One man's story ends with a grave.
The Gospel announces an empty tomb.
Not because Ibzan's life was meaningless.
But because even the most remarkable human life cannot accomplish what Jesus Christ accomplished.
No father, no judge, no ruler, no religious leader can save the human soul by earthly achievement.
Only Christ can reconcile sinners to God.
Jesus said:
“I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.”
— John 6:35, KJV
The Greek expression is:
Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς
Egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs.
“I am the bread of life.”
Jesus was not promising that believers would never experience physical hunger or earthly hardship.
He was revealing Himself as the One who gives the spiritual life and lasting satisfaction that the world cannot provide.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear today.
You have been feeding everybody else.
Making sure the bills are paid.
Making sure the children are cared for.
Making sure your family appears strong.
Making sure your responsibilities are fulfilled.
But somewhere along the way, your own soul has become exhausted.
You have been trying to survive on achievement.
On approval.
On productivity.
On the hope that one more accomplishment will finally make you feel worthy.
And Jesus is calling you away from the impossible task of saving yourself through performance.
Come to Him.
Not after you have fixed everything.
Not after your marriage looks perfect.
Not after your children become everything you hoped they would be.
Not after you have erased every embarrassing chapter of your past.
Come to Him because you need mercy.
The Gospel does not teach that your failures are insignificant.
Sin is serious.
Pride destroys.
Unrepentance hardens the heart.
Bitterness poisons relationships.
Hidden wrongdoing can wound entire families.
But the cross of Jesus Christ tells us that sin is not something God simply overlooks.
Christ bore the penalty of sin, and through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who repent and believe.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not permission to continue living in rebellion.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and return to the God who is faithful to forgive.
And perhaps the greatest gift you can give your family is not the appearance of perfection.
It is the testimony of genuine transformation.
Let your children see that when you sin, you repent.
When you hurt someone, you seek reconciliation.
When you are afraid, you pray.
When you do not understand God's providence, you continue trusting His character.
When you fall, you do not call darkness light.
You return to Jesus.
Because a Christ-centered home is not a home where nobody ever fails.
It is a home where the truth of Christ is honored, sin is taken seriously, forgiveness is practiced, and grace is never confused with permission to do wrong.
Perhaps your family has already suffered deeply.
Perhaps you are estranged from a child.
Perhaps your marriage has endured betrayal.
Perhaps your parents never showed you the love you needed.
Perhaps the word “family” brings more grief than comfort.
Then hear this carefully.
Your past does not have to be the final authority over your future.
You cannot rewrite history.
You cannot force another person to repent.
You cannot guarantee that every broken relationship will be restored in this lifetime.
But through Christ, you can begin walking in truth today.
You can repent where you have sinned.
You can seek help where you have been wounded.
You can establish wise boundaries where necessary.
You can forgive without pretending evil was acceptable.
You can entrust unresolved grief to the Lord.
And you can refuse to let shame convince you that God has no further purpose for your life.
That is the heartbeat of this ministry.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
But because the grace of God can redeem sinners, transform hearts, and bring new life where guilt and hopelessness once ruled.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
The Greek begins:
εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις
Ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis.
“If anyone is in Christ, [there is] a new creation.”
The emphasis is not on human self-improvement.
It is on the transforming reality of belonging to Christ.
You are not saved because you finally built an impressive family.
You are not accepted by God because your children became successful.
You are not justified because you supported a ministry, purchased Christian products, or accumulated religious achievements.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And this grace changes how we live.
It teaches us to honor God with our relationships, our resources, our time, our responsibilities, and the opportunities He places before us.
It also changes how we give.
We do not give money to purchase God's approval.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, generous, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Every article that reaches a struggling believer.
Every biblical resource that helps someone understand Scripture.
Every testimony that reminds a wounded person of God's mercy.
Every Gospel message shared with someone who has never understood why Jesus died and rose again.
These are opportunities worth investing in.
Not out of guilt.
Not because your salvation depends on it.
But because you believe the Gospel is worth proclaiming, and you want to participate in helping this ministry continue and expand.
They are simply a tangible expression of appreciation for those who help make the work possible.
Because the real reward is not merchandise.
It is the privilege of participating in work intended to make Christ known.
You never know who is reading silently.
A father who has not spoken to his son in years.
A mother carrying guilt over mistakes she cannot undo.
A young person who believes their family history has ruined their future.
A Christian who looks strong on Sunday but cries alone during the week.
Someone who has almost given up on the possibility of forgiveness.
You might never know what happens after they read it.
But a simple share can place a message of biblical hope before someone who needs to hear it.
And perhaps there is one person in particular who came to mind while you were reading.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their private struggles.
But to remind them that their story is not beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
And if this message uncovered something in your own heart, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
You do not have to tell the world the details of your pain.
You do not have to publicly confess private sins.
Not as a religious performance.
As a simple testimony that you are not finished seeking the Lord.
We need more than impressive Christian appearances.
We need communities where truth and compassion can exist together.
Where repentance is encouraged.
Where people can ask for prayer without becoming entertainment.
Where the wounded are treated with dignity.
Where Jesus Christ, not human personalities, remains the center.
Read it again when you feel pressured to prove that your life matters.
Invite the believer who has grown spiritually cold.
Invite the person who is searching for truth.
Invite the friend who has never understood the Gospel.
Invite someone who needs to discover that Christianity is not about pretending to be righteous, but about being reconciled to God through the righteousness of Christ.
Make use of these resources.
Study the Scriptures.
Test every teaching against God's Word.
Grow in a faithful local church.
Seek mature Christian fellowship.
Let your faith become more than something you read about on a screen.
Let it shape how you speak to your spouse.
How you raise your children.
How you handle money.
How you respond when offended.
How you confess sin.
How you love people who cannot repay you.
How you live when nobody is watching.
Because one day, just like Ibzan, your earthly story will come to an end.
Your position will belong to someone else.
Your possessions will be distributed.
Your photographs may eventually fade.
Even your name may disappear from the memories of future generations.
But that does not mean your life is meaningless.
The Lord sees what history overlooks.
He sees the quiet act of obedience.
The prayer whispered through tears.
The apology that required courage.
The temptation resisted when nobody would have known.
The sacrifice made out of love.
The truth spoken with gentleness.
The ordinary faithfulness that never becomes a headline.
And above all, He knows those who belong to Him.
Ibzan's account ends with his death and burial.
But the Christian's hope rests in the One who conquered death.
Jesus said:
“Because I live, ye shall live also.”
— John 14:19, KJV
That is where our confidence belongs.
Not in the size of our families.
Not in the number of our achievements.
Not in how many people recognize our names.
But in the crucified and risen Savior.
So before you close this article, ask yourself something.
What are you building that will matter beyond your own lifetime?
And even more importantly…
Are you trusting in what you have built, or in the Lord Jesus Christ who alone can save you?
If you have wandered from Him, turn back.
If you have been hiding sin, repent.
If you have been trying to earn His love through religious performance, remember the sufficiency of Christ's finished work.
If you have been consumed with leaving your children an impressive inheritance, consider the priceless value of leaving them a faithful witness to the Gospel.
You may not have sixty children.
You may never lead a nation.
You may never be remembered in a history book.
But you can live a life that bears witness to Jesus.
And if your family story is marked by scandal, grief, failure, or regret, do not make your past the final chapter.
Bring it into the light of Christ.
The Savior who died for sinners and rose again is able to forgive, restore, and transform those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because the greatest tragedy is not dying with a name the world forgets. It is spending your life building everything except a relationship with the Savior who offers eternal life.
